Seminar Title:

Rational Design of g-C3N4-based Heterojunction Composites for the Photocatalytic Degradation of Emerging Contaminants

Abstract:

The widespread occurrence of emerging contaminants (ECs), including pharmaceutical residues, synthetic dyes, pesticides, endocrine-disrupting compounds, and phenolic pollutants, has become a major environmental concern due to their persistence, toxicity, and poor removal by conventional wastewater treatment processes. The continuous release of ECs into aquatic environments demands efficient and sustainable remediation technologies. Among the available advanced oxidation processes, visible-light-driven semiconductor photocatalysis has emerged as a promising approach for the degradation and mineralization of these ECs using solar energy. Graphitic carbon nitride (g-C₃N₄) has gained considerable attention as a metal-free photocatalyst because of its suitable band gap, visible-light activity, chemical stability, and cost-effective synthesis. However, its practical application is restricted by rapid electron&ndashhole recombination, limited visible-light absorption, and insufficient active catalytic sites. The present research aims to develop rationally designed g-C₃N₄-based heterojunction composites through interface engineering to improve charge separation and enhance visible-light-driven photocatalytic activity. The efficiency of the developed heterojunctions will be evaluated for the degradation of p-nitrophenol (PNP) and PFAS (per and polyfluoroalkyl substances) under visible-light irradiation by investigating the effects of catalyst dosage, pollutant concentration, solution pH, coexisting ions, and water matrices. Furthermore, catalyst stability, reusability, and degradation mechanisms will be investigated to assess their practical applicability. The findings are expected to contribute to the rational design of efficient and reusable g-C₃N₄-based heterojunction photocatalysts for sustainable wastewater treatment and environmental remediation.
